html:
OPIc AL Strategy Guide (문법·전략 총정리)

Target: AL (Advanced Low). This guide is built from personal notes + the ACTFL Advanced-Low descriptor.

How to use it: every case file has a Backbone — your own sentences assembled into one complete

spoken answer, labeled by role. Shadow the backbone for structure — then answer live with new content. Everything left over is a **Phrase

Bank — reusable pieces for other questions. Case-specific Watch-points** flag the grammar the raters

will hear in THAT answer. Do not recite scripts word-for-word; drill the structures, generate content live.

1. How OPIc scoring works (시험 구조와 채점)

  • ~40-minute recorded computer interview; questions come from your Background Survey.
  • Levels: IL → IM (1–3) → IH → AL. The IH→AL jump is the goal.
  • The AL descriptor, concretely: narrate/describe in all major time frames (past · present ·

future) in paragraph-length discourse; **connect sentences with conjunctions so they flow as one

discourse; handle a complication** (unexpected turn) in a familiar situation. AL vocabulary tip:

varied adjectives (see §10).

  • "Errors do not interfere" = patterns matter, not slips. One dropped plural -s is nothing;

dropping it on every countable noun is a pattern — patterns block AL.

LevelWhat the rater hears
ILShort sentences, one at a time. Present tense mostly. Long pauses, restarts.
IMStrings of 2–3 sentences on familiar topics, but time frames mix and the links are "and / then / so".
IHConfident on familiar topics and routine situations; a complication can still cause breakdown. Narration connects, but is not fully sustained.
ALParagraph-length answers in all time frames, sentences connected with transitions, a complication resolved, varied vocabulary. Errors exist but never block the message.

Combo structure (콤보 구조)

  • Questions come in sets of 3 (after the self-intro). PE = Past Experience · RP = Role Play.
  • Set 2: Description → Comparison → PE. 2nd = Comparison ⇒ Set 2 confirmed: 3rd = PE.
  • Set 3: Description → PE → PE/Comparison. 2nd = PE ⇒ 3rd undecided.
  • Description/Habit: aim ~60 s. PE/Comparison: aim 60–90 s — more time to show the AL features.
  • When a question arrives: identify the category first, then pick your MP (main point).

MP ≈ 30 seconds: What + Feeling + Why. Habit answers include at least one of the three.

  • Housing/Home and first-question Description/Habit come up often — prepare them cold if you selected them in the survey.
  • RP11 (survey, 3–4 questions): know the channel (voice message / phone call / in person). On a

call, imagine the other side's replies and respond; on a voicemail, leave all your questions in one message.

  • RP12 (complication): explain the problem clearly, then offer alternatives — ask Q1 → imagine

"No, unfortunately ~" → pivot "Then could I at least ~?" → imagine "Yes, of course." → thank.

  • RP13 (problem/solution PE): don't wait to be asked — the problem is your MP, then the solution experience.
  • IHU14/15 (final survey block): 14 = Comparison (past↔now, or A/B) · 15 = Society / people questions.
  • PE feels real if you went with family or friends — that gives you the quotation for free.
  • Over-rehearsal caps the rating (ACTFL): drill structures, generate content live.

2. Transitions (전환어) — priority 1

Connectors are a scored AL feature. Learn them by FUNCTION — pick 2–3 per function and use them in

every answer until they are automatic. Rows appear in drill order (must-know first).

Written-register words (thus, therefore, in addition…) — see 2.18.

2.1 Starting

PhraseNote
Let me just talk about ~clean, confident opener
The main thing is ~signals the main point
To keep it short / put simplybuys time, promises structure
I'd like to talk about ~safe, slightly formal
What I wanna say is ~casual, natural
If I'm honest / Straight upconfident, casual
Let me cut to the chaseworks best mid-answer, after some context
Here's the bottom line / I'll be upfrontconclusion first
Generally speakinggeneral-fact questions
That's an interesting question, let me think…stall when you need a second

2.2 Contrast: past ↔ now (Comparison questions)

  • Back then, ~ / Nowadays, ~ · In the past / Back in the day → These days / Nowadays
  • Compared to the past, people ~ much more these days.
  • However, ~ · Things are completely different now. / The biggest difference is ~.

2.3 Habit / Description

  • Usually, I ~, but every once in a while, I ~.
  • What I normally do is ~ · Most of the time, I ~ · When I have free time, I ~
  • Whenever / Wherever ~, I always ~ · No matter what happens, I ~ · Every time ~, I ~

2.4 Past experience (sequencing a story)

  • So, this happened a few years ago, when I was ~.
  • At first, ~ → But then, out of nowhere, ~ → In the end, everything worked out.
  • Looking back on it now, I still remember how ~.
  • He/I was like, "~" — the quotation move for PE.

2.5 Wrapping up

  • So that's basically how/why ~ · Anyway, that's my routine.
  • Overall, I really enjoy ~ing. · Personally, I find it relaxing.
  • For me, ~ is a great way to relax.
  • ⚠ rotate closers — never the same one twice in a set (the bank in 2.6 exists for that).
  • ⚠ "relieve stress" is the most overused closer line — swap it: clear my head / unwind / hit the reset button.

2.6 Natural endings — closing bank (by answer type)

One compound sentence (10–15 words) is enough to close. Drop one crisp line, let your voice fall at

the end, click Next. Never reuse the same closer across a set.

Habit / description answers

LineFilled example
Honestly, my ~ just doesn't feel complete without ___.Honestly, my weekend just doesn't feel complete without sitting at my local cafe with an iced Frappuccino.
It's basically how I hit the reset button after a long ___.The gym right after work is basically how I hit the reset button and leave all my stress behind.
It's nothing fancy, but it's easily the best part of my ___.Evening walks in the park are nothing fancy, but they're easily the best part of my day.
I don't see myself giving this up anytime soon.Even when I'm exhausted, I always read a few pages before bed — I don't see myself giving that up anytime soon.
So yeah, that's pretty much what my typical ___ looks like.Grabbing a book and zoning out on public transit is pretty much what my daily commute looks like.

Past experience answers

LineFilled example
Looking back, it still stands out as one of the best decisions I've made.Signing up for that reading club on a whim still stands out as one of the best decisions I've made this year.
It was a total mess at the time, but hey — at least I got a good story out of it.Getting lost in China was stressful at the time, but hey, at least I got a great story out of it.
We still talk about it all the time — I'd do it all over again in a heartbeat.My friends and I still talk about that trip all the time, and I'd do it all over again in a heartbeat.
That experience really changed the way I look at ___.That trip really changed the way I look at traveling — I never miss my workout now, even on vacation.
I haven't been back since, but it's at the top of my list.I haven't been back to China since, but going back is at the top of my list for next year.

Comparison (past ↔ now) answers

LineFilled example
I'm so glad I made the switch — I can't imagine going back.I'm so glad I traded late-night TV for reading; I can't imagine going back to my old routine.
The difference is just night and day.Since I started working out regularly, the difference in my energy is just night and day.
I guess my priorities have shifted as I've gotten older.I used to love crowded downtown spots — now I just want a quiet park. I guess my priorities have shifted a bit.
It took some getting used to, but now it's second nature.Sorting the recycling took some getting used to, but now it's just second nature.
Both have their perks, but ~ suits me way better now.Driving had its perks, of course, but reading on the subway suits my life way better now.

Opinion / technology answers

LineFilled example
At the end of the day, it all comes down to ___.My phone makes life super convenient, sure — but at the end of the day, it comes down to knowing when to unplug.
I hate to admit it, but I'd be lost without ___.I hate to admit it, but without the map apps on my phone, I'd be completely lost in a new city.
It's wild how fast things are changing — I'm curious where we'll be in five years.It's wild how fast tech is changing — I'm curious to see where we'll be in five years.
For better or worse, it's a huge part of life now.For better or worse, it's a huge part of life now — so we might as well make the most of it.

Recommendation closers (talk to the interviewer like a person)

LineFilled example
If you ever find yourself in ___, you owe it to yourself to ___.If you ever find yourself in Korea in spring, you owe it to yourself to spend a few days in Jeju.
Give it a shot sometime — you might be surprised.If you haven't joined a reading club, give it a shot sometime — you might be surprised how much you get into it.
Take my word for it: skip ___, go straight for ___.Take my word for it: skip the regular coffee and go straight for the Vanilla Cream Cold Brew.

Time-up / graceful exit

LineFilled example
Anyway, I could go on and on about this, but that's the gist of it.Anyway, I could go on and on about my gym routine, but that's the gist of it.
So yeah — that's pretty much the whole story.We made our flight back with five minutes to spare — so yeah, that's pretty much the whole story.
And yeah… that's about all there is to say on that.Recycling here is a bit of a chore, for sure — and yeah, that's about all there is to say on that.
I feel like I'm rambling, so I'll leave it at that.There are a million other reasons I love public transit, but I feel like I'm rambling, so I'll leave it at that.

Three closers to avoid (they scream "memorized script")

  1. "In conclusion / To sum up" — nobody says that in a conversation.
  2. "It helps me relieve my stress" as every ending — swap: clear my head / unwind / hit the reset button.
  3. "Thank you for listening to my story." — you're chatting with the interviewer, not giving a speech.

2.7 Referring back inside a combo set (콤보 연결)

Combo questions are RELATED — a callback shows discourse control. Use it when it fits naturally.

  • As I mentioned before, ~
  • I think I mentioned this already, but ~
  • Like I said earlier / in the previous question, ~
  • Going back to what I said before, ~
  • To build on what I just said, ~
  • The same thing happened when ~

2.8 Hard question / stalling

  • Wow, that's quite a tough question. / I didn't expect such a hard question.
  • Let me think for a second… / How should I put this…
  • As far as I know, ~ (when you're not sure)

2.9 돌발 (unexpected) / framing

  • To tell you the truth, ~ · Here in Korea, ~ · People often say that ~
  • The bottom line is that ~ · This is crucial because ~
  • The good/best thing is that ~ · The reason is/was that ~ (= because)

2.10 Adding information / giving examples

TransitionExample
For example / For instanceI try to exercise in small ways; for instance, I take the stairs instead of the elevator.
Such asI like reading books about travel, such as stories about people exploring China.
BesidesI like that cafe because it's quiet, and besides, it's close to my apartment.
On top of thatThe gym is affordable, and on top of that, it's open late.
Another thing is…Another thing is, the cafe staff always remember my usual Frappuccino order.
PlusThe reading club meets twice a month — plus, we chat online between meetings.
What's moreThe park is close to my place, and what's more, it's rarely crowded in the morning.

2.11 Cause & result

TransitionExample
SoIt started raining during my Jeju trip, so I ducked into a cafe.
That's why (already collected)I spend a lot of time looking at screens, and that's why I like taking walks in the park.
Because of thatThe subway was delayed, and because of that, I was late for my reading club.
Thanks to + nounThanks to my phone's translation app, ordering food in China was much easier.
Which is whyMy neighborhood is really walkable, which is why I don't use my car very often.
As a resultI started working out regularly, and as a result, I have more energy during the day.
Due to + nounDue to the heavy rain, we changed our plans — spoken: because of the heavy rain

2.12 Sequence / time — extended bank (extends 2.4)

TransitionExample
ThenWe grabbed coffee, and then we went for a walk around the park.
After thatI visited a market in China, and after that, I tried some local street food.
EventuallyI got lost in Jeju, but eventually, I found my way back to the hotel.
FinallyAfter checking a few different cafes, I finally found one with an open table.
All of a suddenI was walking in the park when, all of a sudden, it started pouring.
The next thing I knew…I fell asleep on the bus, and the next thing I knew, I'd missed my stop.
AfterwardI worked out at the gym and grabbed a smoothie afterward.
In the meantimeMy friend was running late, so in the meantime, I ordered a Frappuccino.
Out of the blueOut of the blue, a friend from my reading club invited me to join her on a trip to Jeju.

2.13 Emphasis

TransitionExample
Actually (counter-expectation)I actually enjoy taking the subway, because I can read during the ride.
In factI go to that cafe all the time; in fact, I was there just yesterday.
The thing is…The thing is, my gym gets so crowded after work that I prefer going in the morning.
What's really + adjective + is…What's really nice about my neighborhood is that there's a park just around the corner.
Believe it or notBelieve it or not, I finished a whole book on the flight to China.

2.14 Concession — "I know, but…"

TransitionExample
Even thoughEven though it rained in Jeju, I still had a great trip.
StillThe subway was crowded, but it was still faster than driving.
I know, but…The gym is pretty expensive — I know, but I use it almost every day.
Having said thatThe gym can get crowded; having said that, the equipment is great.
That saidI love my phone; that said, I probably spend too much time on it.
Even soThe cafe was packed; even so, we managed to find a table.

2.15 Saying it another way

TransitionExample
What I mean is…I like cafes with character; what I mean is, I prefer places that feel cozy and personal.
BasicallyI follow all the building's waste rules; basically, I sort my recycling at home and take it downstairs once a week.
In other wordsMy phone is my travel guide; in other words, I use it for maps, translations, and restaurant recommendations.
To put it another wayThe reading club keeps me motivated; to put it another way, it gives me a reason to finish books.

2.16 Shifting to a related point

TransitionExample
Speaking of whichI love walking in the park. Speaking of the park, there's a great cafe right next to it.
When it comes to…When it comes to working out, I prefer going in the morning.
In terms of…In terms of public transit, my neighborhood is really convenient.
As for…As for my favorite drink, I usually go for a Frappuccino.

2.17 Condition / hypothetical

TransitionExample
If I had to choose…If I had to choose, I'd visit Jeju again rather than go somewhere new.
If I get the chance…If I get the chance, I'd love to visit China again.
As long as…As long as the weather's nice, I'll walk to the park.
Unless…I take the subway unless I'm carrying something really heavy.

2.18 Formal words — thus, therefore, hence, moreover, nevertheless

These are correct but sound essay-like spoken out loud. Use sparingly — the spoken alternative is

easier to say and scores the same.

FormalSpoken replacementExample (formal)
thusso / that's whyThe subway was delayed, and thus I arrived late at the cafe.
thereforeso / that's whyThe gym was closed; therefore, I went for a walk instead.
hencesoI missed my bus, so I had a long walk home.
moreoveron top of thatThe cafe is quiet; moreover, it's close to my apartment.
neverthelessstill / even soIt rained during our Jeju trip; nevertheless, we had a great time.

2.19 Master review drill (patterns from 2.11–2.17 + new frames)

PatternFilled example
When it comes to ___, I ___.When it comes to coffee, I usually order a Frappuccino.
The more ___, the more ___.The more I read, the more I want to discuss books with other people.
It depends on ___, but usually ___.It depends on the weather, but usually I walk to the park after dinner.
If I had to choose, I'd ___.If I had to choose, I'd take the subway instead of driving.
Speaking of ___, ___.Speaking of Jeju, I'd love to go back and explore more of the island.
In terms of ___, ___.In terms of recycling, my apartment building makes it pretty easy.
What I love about ___ is ___.What I love about my neighborhood is that everything I need is within walking distance.
___, which is why ___.I wanted to try local food in China, which is why I visited a street market.
Not only ___, but ___ too.Not only is my gym close to home, but it's affordable too.
Having said that, ___.My phone is really useful. Having said that, I try not to use it during meals.

2.20 A/B contrast (two things, not past/present)

TransitionExample
On the other hand, ~The subway is crowded. On the other hand, it's cheap and always on time.
Whereas ~, ~I used to drive everywhere, whereas now I read on the bus.
Unlike ~, ~Unlike my old neighborhood, everything here is walkable.
Compared with ~, ~Compared with my old phone, this one is huge.

2.21 Complication — the AL key

TransitionExample
Unfortunately, ~Unfortunately, the cafe was full when we got there.
To make matters worse, ~The bus was late, and to make matters worse, it started raining.
Luckily / It turned out that ~Luckily, my friend knew a place nearby. / It turned out that the show was canceled.
I had no idea what to doAt first, I had no idea what to do.

2.22 Listing (advantages / reasons)

TransitionExample
First of all, ~ / Second, ~ / Lastly, ~First of all, it's close to my place. Second, the price is fair.
One advantage is ~; another is ~One advantage is convenience; another is the price.

2.23 Opinion + future (IHU15 / plans)

TransitionExample
In my opinion, ~In my opinion, reading is the best habit you can build.
I tend to think ~I tend to think technology does more good than harm.
A lot of people say ~, but I ~A lot of people say gyms are boring, but I enjoy mine.
I'm planning to ~ / I'm going to ~I'm planning to visit Jeju this spring.

3. Tense (시제) — priority 2

  • Specific past time ⇒ simple past, never present perfect.

X: I have visited Busan last summer. → O: I visited Busan last summer.

Present perfect for no specific time OR duration: "I've been to Busan a few times." / "I've worked here for five years."

  • used to = a repeated past habit that stopped — the Comparison answer:

"I used to X. But these days, I Y." / "I don't X as often as I used to."

  • Narration drill: anchor = simple past. Shift only twice — past perfect for before-the-story

("By the time I got there, it had already closed") and present for the closing reflection

("Now, whenever I ~, I laugh"). Record one story; listen for tense slips only; re-record.

Never restart on a slip — note it, keep talking.

4. Plurals (복수형) — priority 3

Four templates cover most spoken cases:

  1. one of the + PLURAL + singular verb: "One of the things I like most is ~" / "One of my friends lives in Busan."
  2. many / most / several / a few / a couple of + PLURAL: "Many students study there."
  3. I like / enjoy + PLURAL category: "I like action movies" — mass nouns stay singular: "I enjoy music."
  4. Irregulars, no extra -s: children, people, men, women, feet, teeth.

Uncountable traps (no -s; count with "a piece of"):

WrongRight
furnitures, advicesfurniture, advice — a piece of furniture / advice
informations, softwaresinformation, software
equipments, luggagesequipment, luggage
homeworks, newseshomework, news

Self-check: after any quantity word, pronounce the -s deliberately.

5. Articles (관사) — priority 4

  • First mention = a/an → every mention after = the: "I went to a cafe near my house. The

cafe was sleek, and the barista was friendly."

  • the for unique/context-known: the subway, the bus, the weather, the internet,

the gym (the one you go to), the park near my house.

  • Zero article for plural/uncountable generalities: "I like books." / "I listen to music."
  • Fix actively: "I have a dog." / "I went to the gym." (Korean drops these.)
  • the also when the context makes it obvious: "I went to a cafe. The barista was friendly."

6. Other pattern risks

  • he / she: Korean pronouns are gender-neutral — decide the person's gender in the first sentence of

a story and keep it. Mixing mid-story is a classic Korean-L1 pattern error.

  • in / on / at: in the morning / in Korea · on Monday / on the weekend · at night / at 7 p.m.
  • discuss takes no "about": "we discussed the plan". · agree with a person, agree on a plan.
  • interested in (~에 관심 있는) vs interesting (~흥미로운) — people ARE interested; things ARE interesting.

7. 말 늘리기 — the MP framework (expanding any answer)

MovePhrases
MP · CurrentWhat is it + Feeling (like/dislike) + Reason (The reason is that ~ / because ~)
Past (opposite)In the past, I ~ / Back in the day, I used to ~ (say the OPPOSITE of your MP)
Current againHowever, ~ / These days, ~ / Nowadays, ~

Fillers (in moderation — clusters of hesitation count as disfluency): well / you know / I mean / let me see…

Quotes for PE: he/I was like, "~".

Frames: The good/best thing is that ~ · the reason is/was that ~ · People often say that ~ ·

This is crucial because ~ · Could/Would you please ~ (requests).

8. Case files (케이스별 모범 답안)

Each case: **Target question → Backbone ([B], shadow as one answer) → Phrase bank ([P], reusable) →

Watch-points → Past variation → Related questions.** Your own sentences, in speaking order.

8.1 음료 — Favorite drink

Target: "What drinks do you enjoy? How do you choose?"

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] I usually choose my drink depending on my mood.
  2. [B · MP] I often order a Frappuccino.
  3. [B · Detail] It's a very sweet drink, and it's quite popular in Korea.
  4. [B · Feeling] Personally, I like it because it's good for relaxing, especially when I'm stressed from work.
  5. [B · MP] Another drink I like is the Vanilla Cream Cold Brew.
  6. [B · Contrast] It's also sweet, but it's not as sweet as a Frappuccino.
  7. [B · Detail] And it has less sugar and fewer calories.
  8. [B · Wrap] So, I enjoy both drinks, but I choose between them depending on my mood.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] I usually choose ___ depending on my mood.
  • [P · Feeling] I like it because it's good for relaxing.
  • [P · Contrast] It's sweet, but it's not as sweet as ___.
  • [P · Comparison] It has less sugar and fewer calories.

Watch-points

  • less sugar (uncountable) vs fewer calories (countable plural) — you already have this right; keep it.
  • not as sweet as — the comparison pattern for two things.

Past variation (your notes don't say what you drank before — fill this in before shadowing):

"In the past, I usually ordered ___. These days, I order a Frappuccino or Vanilla Cream Cold Brew, depending on my mood."

Related questions: "Describe a drink you often order." (backbone 2–4) · "Compare two drinks you

like." (5–8) · "What do you order when you're stressed?" (4 + a personal example).

8.2 카페 — Starbucks

Target: "Describe your favorite cafe. What do you do there?"

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] There is a great cafe near my place that I go to all the time — a Starbucks.
  2. [B · Detail] It's a big four-story building.
  3. [B · Detail] The first floor is a little bit noisy, but it's lively and full of energy.
  4. [B · Detail] The higher floors are quiet, so there are many students there.
  5. [B · Detail] It's cozy and sleek with modern lighting.
  6. [B · Detail] I love their food and drinks — a lot of people in Korea love Frappuccinos.
  7. [B · Detail] Their Vanilla Cream Cold Brew is low in sugar and low in calories.
  8. [B · MP] I love reading books there — that's why I go.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] There is a great ___ near my place that I go to.
  • [P · Detail] It's located not far from where I live.
  • [P · Feeling] I love reading books there.

Watch-points

  • a cafe (first mention) → the first floor / the higher floors (specific parts of that known building).
  • "a four-story building" — hyphenated when it describes a noun.
  • "low in sugar and low in calories."

Related questions: "Describe your neighborhood." (the opener + location lines) · "Where do you read

books?" (wrap + the reading case below).

8.3 취미/독서 — Reading

Target: "Tell me about a hobby you enjoy."

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] I often read books as a hobby — I love books.
  2. [B · Detail] I always concentrate when I read books.
  3. [B · Detail] I get immersed in the story — I always feel like I become the main character when I read novels.
  4. [B · Detail] As for where I like to read — bookstores have a warm atmosphere, and libraries are always quiet and friendly when I go there.
  5. [B · Detail] On top of that, I'm in a reading club.
  6. [B · Contrast] Joining the reading club was easy, but at first, it felt unfamiliar.
  7. [B · Contrast] In the past, I didn't like reading popular books.
  8. [B · Detail] However, I once bought a bestseller and enjoyed it.
  9. [B · Wrap] These days, I prefer popular books — that's why reading has become an important part of my life.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Past] I didn't really have a hobby when I was younger — I just watched TV.
  • [P · Past] I couldn't concentrate on books when I was younger.
  • [P · Feeling] I can focus well with some background noise.
  • [P · Frame] I really enjoy ___ in my free time. / One of my favorite activities is ___.
  • [P · Feeling] I especially/absolutely like ___ because it helps me relax.
  • [P · Feeling] It's a great way to relieve stress. / It makes me feel relaxed/energetic/refreshed.
  • [P · Wrap] For me, ___ is a great way to relax.

Watch-points

  • enjoy + -ing: "I enjoy reading", not "enjoy to read".
  • "Joining the reading club was easy" — the -ing phrase is the subject.
  • resolved: the past is "just watched TV" · "typical books" → popular books / a bestseller — keep your category consistent.

Past variation: "In the past, my hobby was watching TV. I couldn't concentrate on books when I was

younger, and I didn't like reading typical books. However, I once bought a more typical book and enjoyed

it — these days, I prefer them."

Related questions: "Tell me about your reading club." (6–7 + what members do) · "Describe a place

where you read." (4–5) · "How has your hobby changed?" (past variation) · "Tell me about a book you

enjoyed." (9 + title/content/reaction — add your own).

8.4 동료와 대화 — Coffee breaks at work

Target: "What do you and your co-workers talk about during breaks?"

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] During coffee breaks, I usually talk about new technology with my co-workers.
  2. [B · Reason] That's because we develop software for robotics and automation.
  3. [B · Example] For example, I sometimes ask them, "Hey, have you checked out the latest Physical AI solutions?"
  4. [B · Quote] They might say, "Not yet. What are they about?"
  5. [B · Detail] Then I explain the new solutions to them.
  6. [B · Feeling] My co-workers are usually very interested, so we enjoy discussing them.
  7. [B · Wrap] That's what we usually talk about during coffee breaks.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] During coffee breaks, I usually talk about ___ with my co-workers.
  • [P · Example] For example, I sometimes ask them, "___?"
  • [P · Wrap] That's what we usually talk about during ~.

Watch-points

  • interested (사람이 관심 있는) — not "interesting".
  • After the quotation, add ONE sentence explaining what the new thing actually does (that's your sentence 5).

Related questions: "Tell me about your co-workers." · "What do you do at lunch time?" (same skeleton,

different topic — the frames transfer).

8.5 교통수단 — Public transportation

Target: "How do you get around? Do you use public transportation?"

Backbone

  1. [B · MP] I love how I can read something while taking public transit.
  2. [B · Feeling] On busy workdays, it's almost the only time I can actually read.
  3. [B · Contrast] It's funny, because I never liked reading before.
  4. [B · Past] In the past, I drove everywhere / I didn't take the bus much. *(fill in your real past)*
  5. [B · Wrap] These days, I take public transit every day — and I read.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] I love how I can ___ while ~ing.
  • [P · Contrast] It's interesting because I didn't ~ before. / I've never liked ~ before.

Watch-points

  • "on public transit" (no "the" needed for the general mode).
  • "I never liked reading before" — simple past, because that state is over (you enjoy reading now).

Related questions: "Tell me about the subway in your city." · "How has transportation changed?"

(the comparison frames).

8.6 재활용 — Recycling

Target: "Do you recycle at home? Tell me about it."

Backbone

  1. [B · MP] I'm meticulous about recycling.
  2. [B · Detail] It's really rare for me to forget to sort the recycling.
  3. [B · Contrast] It's funny, because I didn't recycle much before.
  4. [B · Past] I just threw everything away — I didn't separate anything. *(adjust to your real habit)*
  5. [B · Wrap] These days I separate everything carefully.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] It's really rare for me to forget to ~.
  • [P · Contrast] It's interesting because I didn't ~ frequently before.

Watch-points

  • meticulous (꼼꼼한) — say it: meh-TIC-u-lus. + meticulous about ~ing.
  • "sort the recycling" (분리수거하다).

Related questions: "How do people recycle in Korea?" · "Has recycling changed compared to the past?"

(comparison frames + these lines).

8.7 가구 — Furniture

Target: "Describe the furniture in your home. What's your favorite piece?"

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] I'll focus on one piece of furniture that I love.
  2. [B · Detail] My apartment is small but cozy.
  3. [B · MP] In the living room, there is a big wooden table where I read books.
  4. [B · Contrast] When I was young, I loved TV — I wasted too much time on it.
  5. [B · Wrap] But these days, I sit at that table and read instead.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Opener] To keep this answer short, I'll focus on ~.
  • [P · Detail] My apartment is small but cozy.

Watch-points

  • furniture is uncountable: "one piece of furniture", never "a furniture".
  • "a big wooden table" — material adjective before the noun.

Past variation: built into the backbone (TV → table) — this case IS a comparison.

Related questions: "Describe your living room." · "What's in your apartment?" (backbone + your own details).

8.8 동네 — Neighborhood

Target: "Describe your neighborhood. What do you like about it?"

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] When I first moved into my place, everything was brand new — a little unfamiliar.
  2. [B · Contrast] These days, though, I'm used to it — there are sleek cafes everywhere.
  3. [B · MP] There is a great cafe not far from where I live.
  4. [B · Wrap] That's why I like my neighborhood.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] ~ is located not far from where I live.

Watch-points

  • "moved into my house" · "brand new".
  • "There is a great place" — singular verb after "there".

Related questions: "Has your neighborhood changed?" (brand new → these days) · "What do people do

in your neighborhood?" (cafe case joins here).

8.9 음악 — Music

Target: "Tell me about the music you like. Do you go to concerts?"

Backbone

  1. [B · MP] I like pop — especially American pop, because those songs cheer me up.
  2. [B · Detail] I love one songwriter's music in particular.
  3. [B · Detail] He writes great melodies and lyrics, and most of his songs are very popular in Korea.
  4. [B · Detail] I often go to his concerts.
  5. [B · Detail] I also go to classical concerts pretty often, such as symphonies or piano recitals.
  6. [B · Wrap] That's why music has become an important part of my life.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Feeling] Their songs cheer me up.
  • [P · Frame] I love ___'s music because he writes ___.

Watch-points

  • Keep he consistent once you name a male composer (he/she mixing is a pattern error).
  • "piano recitals" · "attend a concert" (not "go to a concert of my ~" — simpler).

Related questions: "Tell me about a concert you attended." (PE frames + quotation) · "Do you play an

instrument?" (feeling frames).

8.10 영화 — Movies

Target: "How often do you watch movies? Do you go to the theater?"

Backbone

  1. [B · MP] I usually go to the theater in my neighborhood.
  2. [B · Detail] It's small, with only a few screens, so it's rarely crowded.
  3. [B · Feeling] So I can always watch a movie quietly whenever I want.
  4. [B · Detail] Before I watch one, I read the reviews — for the last film I saw, I had read really good reviews beforehand.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Detail] small with a few screenings / mostly not crowded.
  • [P · Movie] Silver Linings Playbook — I like it because it deals with superstition and praying.
  • [P · Movie] Guardians of the Galaxy — my favorite character is Rocket, the raccoon.
  • [P · Movie] American Sniper — it shows trauma and PTSD after war.

Watch-points

  • "the theater in my neighborhood" — the known one, so "the".
  • "I'd read works only AFTER a past anchor: 'for the last film I saw, I'd read ~'."

Related questions: "Tell me about a movie you recently watched." (pick one of the three films + its

talking point) · "Do you prefer watching at home or at the theater?" (comparison frames).

8.11 공원 — Park

Target: "Is there a park near your home? What do you do there?"

Backbone

  1. [B · MP] I often take a walk in the park near my place.
  2. [B · Detail] There's a walking path, and it takes about 30 minutes to walk around the whole park.
  3. [B · Detail] So I walk a few laps around it.
  4. [B · Detail] I put on some sunblock before I go.
  5. [B · Wrap] Sometimes I spend a whole afternoon there — reading, or just walking.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] It takes about ___ minutes to ~, so I ~.
  • [P · Detail] put on some sunblock / spend a whole afternoon.
  • [P · Scene] I lie down on the grass and read a book.

Watch-points

  • "a few laps" · "put on sunblock" · "spend a whole afternoon there".

Related questions: "What do people do in parks in Korea?" · "Tell me about a memorable day in the

park." (PE frames — your "spent a whole afternoon" line starts it).

8.12 헬스장 — Gym

Target: "Do you exercise? Tell me about your workout routine."

Backbone

  1. [B · MP] I go to the gym at least three times a week to work out — I want to stay in shape.
  2. [B · Contrast] When I first started working out, I got exhausted easily.
  3. [B · Detail] I was a little overweight before I started going to the gym.
  4. [B · Detail] The gym I go to has a lot of exercise equipment, like treadmills.
  5. [B · Detail] At the gym, I first do stretches so I don't get hurt during my workout.
  6. [B · Detail] After I finish running, I do weight training to build muscle.
  7. [B · Feeling] Although I try to do weight training properly, it's often not easy.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] stay fit / keep in shape / never miss my workout.

Watch-points

  • "stay in shape" / "keep in shape".
  • "build muscle" (uncountable here) · "so I don't get hurt" (habitual).
  • equipment uncountable.

Past variation: built into the backbone (overweight → now) — Comparison-ready.

Related questions: "Tell me about your first day at the gym." (PE frames) · "Why do people exercise?"

(society frame) · "How do you feel after a workout?" (feeling frames: refreshed / exhausted).

8.13 해외 여행 — First trip abroad (China, PE)

Target: "Tell me about your first trip abroad."

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] I remember my first trip abroad — it was a school trip to China.
  2. [B · Detail] I don't know why my teachers chose China as our first destination, but I was curious to try it.
  3. [B · Detail] I got my first passport for that trip, because it was my first time outside Korea.
  4. [B · Detail] We used public transportation to get around.
  5. [B · Complication] At first, we couldn't read the menus at all. So my friend was like, "Let's just use a translation app and point!"
  6. [B · Feeling] The food was traditional Chinese — oily but delicious.
  7. [B · Wrap] I even gained weight on that trip. It's not easy to lose weight, so I never miss my workout these days.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] I remember a time when I ___ed. / Something interesting happened when I ~ed.
  • [P · PE] It was one of the most memorable moments of my life.

Watch-points

  • "I got my first passport" — "make a passport" sounds like counterfeiting.
  • "get around" = travel locally.
  • The complication + quote (5) is what makes this PE AL-level — don't drop it.
  • Keep the whole story in simple past; the last line switches to present ("I never miss") — that's the

controlled shift.

Related questions: "What did you eat there?" (5) · "Would you go back?" (trip-plan case) · "What did

you learn from the trip?" ("because of that experience, I learned ~").

8.14 여행 계획 — Domestic trip

Target: "If you take a trip in Korea, where would you go?"

Backbone

  1. [B · MP] I would most likely go to Jeju Island for my domestic trip.
  2. [B · Detail] I always try to pack light — having a heavy suitcase could actually be a big hassle.
  3. [B · Detail] I also pack a first-aid kit whenever I travel.
  4. [B · Wrap] When I get there, I would like to take pictures of the beautiful beaches and nature. *(or say Gyeongju, for the ancient architecture)*

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] I would most likely go to ~.
  • [P · Habit] I always try to pack light whenever I travel.
  • [P · Detail] Having a heavy suitcase could be a big hassle.

Watch-points

  • "pack light" (adverb — "pack lightly" also fine, pick one).
  • "a hassle" — countable.

Related questions: "What do you pack?" (2–3) · "Tell me about a memorable trip." (China PE + callback:

"Unlike my trip to China, ~").

8.15 기후 — Climate

Target: "What's the weather like in Korea?"

Backbone (thin — add one personal detail before memorizing)

  1. [B · MP] In Korea, we have four very distinct seasons.
  2. [B · Detail] When it gets really cold in winter, the water pipes can even freeze.
  3. [B · Detail] Summer is humid, and the rainy season brings a lot of rain at once.

Past variation: "Compared to the past, summers have gotten hotter and longer — we use the air

conditioner a lot more."

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] When it gets really ~, ~ can ~.

Watch-points

  • "the water pipes can freeze" — plural + base verb after can.

Related questions: "How does the weather affect your life?" · "Has the climate changed compared to

the past?" (comparison frames — a possible IHU14 topic).

8.16 기술 — Technology

Target: "How has technology changed your daily life?"

Backbone

  1. [B · Opener] I think technology plays a huge role in our lives.
  2. [B · Detail] Many people use it in their daily lives.
  3. [B · Example] One example is my phone — it's pretty old, but still very usable.
  4. [B · Advantage] One advantage is how much time it saves — I can order food, translate a menu, and navigate a new city from one device.
  5. [B · Disadvantage] However, it also has some disadvantages — some people worry about addiction.
  6. [B · Future] In the future, I think new technology like AI and robotics will become even more common.
  7. [B · Wrap] That's why technology is important in modern society.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Frame] One advantage of ~ is convenience. / However, ~ also has some disadvantages.
  • [P · Frame] Compared to the past, ~ has changed a lot. / Another example of ~ is ~.
  • [P · Future] I believe ~ will continue to grow. / More people will probably use ~.
  • [P · Detail] My phone is pretty old but still very usable.

Watch-points

  • advantages / disadvantages — plural; stress: dis-ad-VAN-ta-ges.
  • "compared to the past".

Past variation: "Compared to the past, phones have changed a lot — my first phone could only ___.

*(fill in: calls and texts only?)*

Related questions: "Do people rely on technology too much?" (disadvantage line) · "What technology

do you use at work?" (coworker case joins here — Physical AI).

8.17 RP11 — asking questions (survey call)

Target: "You have a chance to ask ~. Call and ask your questions."

Backbone (state the purpose → 3–4 questions → close)

  1. [B · Opener] Hi, I'm calling because I have a question about your gym membership.
  2. [B · Q1] Could you give me some information about the monthly fee?
  3. [B · Q2] What time does the gym open on weekends?
  4. [B · Q3] Do you have any recommendations for a beginner like me?
  5. [B · Close] That sounds great — thank you so much for your help!

Phrase bank

  • [P · Q] I'd like to ask about ~ / What time does ~ start? / How much does ~ cost?
  • [P · Q] Could you explain the details of the ~? / What would you recommend for ~?

Watch-points

  • State the purpose in the FIRST sentence (I'm calling because ~).
  • If the prompt is a voicemail, leave all your questions in one message — don't act out replies.

8.18 RP12 — problem + alternatives

Target: "Your reservation has a problem. Call and solve it."

Backbone (explain the problem → offer alternatives → thank)

  1. [B · Opener] Hello, I'm calling because something went wrong with my booking.
  2. [B · Problem] I reserved a table for Friday night, but I got a text saying it was canceled.
  3. [B · Ask] Could you please check what happened?
  4. [B · Alternative] *(imagine: fully booked)* Then could I at least get a table for Saturday instead?
  5. [B · Close] That would be great — I really appreciate your help with my booking.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Problem] I have a problem with my ~ / I'm not sure what to do about my ~.
  • [P · Alternative] Is it possible to change the ~ time/date? / Could I make a reservation for tomorrow instead?
  • [P · Close] I'm glad we solved the issue. / Thanks again for helping with my ~.

Watch-points

  • Explain the problem FIRST, then offer 2–3 alternatives — don't just complain.
  • Stay polite: "Could/Would you please ~" beats "You must ~".

8.19 RP13 — problem/solution (PE)

Target: "Tell me about a time you solved a problem."

Backbone (frames + one worked example)

  1. [B · Opener] However, I once had a problem when my old phone kept dying by noon.
  2. [B · Feeling] At first, I didn't know how to handle it.
  3. [B · Solution] So I decided to give it a try — I bought a battery pack and changed my settings.
  4. [B · Result] In the end, everything worked out well with the battery issue.
  5. [B · Wrap] Because of that experience, I learned the importance of checking my settings.

Phrase bank

  • [P · Opener] Something unexpected happened when I ~ed.
  • [P · Frame] At first, I didn't know how to handle ~. / In the end, everything worked out well with ~.
  • [P · Wrap] Because of that experience, I learned the importance/limit of ~.

Watch-points

  • Don't wait for the interviewer to ask for the solution — the problem is your MP, the solution is the BODY.
  • The phone story is an EXAMPLE — swap in your own problem before memorizing.

9. Q1 self-introduction model

The self-introduction always comes first (the mock-exam videos skip it — drill it here):

Hi, my name is ___. I'm a software engineer at a company that develops robotics and automation
software. I've been working there for ___ years. Outside of work, I love reading — I'm actually
in a reading club that meets twice a month. These days I'm also trying to stay in shape, so I work
out a few times a week. Anyway, I'm looking forward to this interview — let's get started.

Structure: name → job (+ one detail) → two hooks (reading + gym) → hand-off. 30–40 seconds.

It previews your survey topics and sets an AL tone right away.

10. Adjective upgrades ("varied adjectives" is an AL marker)

WeakUpgrade
very goodfantastic / awesome / amazing
very badterrible / awful
very big / smallhuge / tiny
very tiredexhausted / worn out
very happythrilled / delighted
very interestingfascinating
very cold / hotfreezing / boiling
very surprisedstunned
very funnyhilarious
very importantcrucial / essential
very prettygorgeous

Intensifiers: really / so / absolutely — "I absolutely love it". ⚠ very cannot upgrade extreme

adjectives: ~~very exhausted~~ → absolutely exhausted, ~~very freezing~~ → freezing.

Quantity: a lot of ~ / a bunch of ~ / like a lot.

Praise adjectives: fantastic / amazing / spectacular / wonderful / awesome.

11. Survival kit (blanking out · unknown words)

  • Buying time: Let me think for a second… / How should I put this… / That's a tough one.
  • Unknown word → paraphrase: "It's a thing you use to ~" / "It's like a ~, but for ~" /

"I can't remember the exact word, but it's something that ~".

  • Recovering mid-sentence: "…anyway, what I wanted to say was ~" / "…or something like that."
  • Wrong tense halfway: finish the sentence, put the NEXT sentence back in the anchor tense. Do not restart.
  • Nothing to say: switch to feeling + reason — "Personally, I find it ~ because ~" — a feeling

sentence is always available, for any topic.

12. Final checklist

Do

  • Open with a transition, close with a feeling + "That's why ~".
  • Keep PE / Comparison around 60–90 s; Description/Habit short.
  • One anchor tense per story; used to for every past-vs-now contrast.
  • a on first mention, the after; -s after many / most / several / a few / a couple of.
  • Quote someone in every PE ("I was like, ~") — and go with family/friends in the story.
  • Rotate closers — never the same line twice in a set (the bank in 2.6).
  • Refer back inside combos ("Like I said earlier, ~").
  • If a run wedges: finish the sentence, put the next one back on track. Recovery, not perfection.

Don't

  • Don't recite a memorized script word-for-word (it caps the rating).
  • Don't answer a Comparison with two unrelated facts — contrast them.
  • Don't say "one of my friend" / "I like action movie" / "I went to gym" / "furnitures".
  • Don't leave a silence — fill it with "Let me think for a second…". Fillers are strategy, in moderation.
